# Goal

Compare ordinary random cross-validation with blocked cross-validation for spatially and temporally correlated environmental data.

In this homework, you will use a gridded **sea surface temperature (SST)** dataset. SST is a good example because nearby ocean grid cells tend to have similar temperatures, and nearby months or years are also related. This means ordinary random cross-validation can give an overly optimistic estimate of model performance.

Sections marked **TODO** are places where you should write or modify code.

# 1. Load the Sea Surface Temperature Dataset

The data are stored as a NetCDF file, a common format for gridded environmental and oceanographic data. Instead of rows and columns only, the data have dimensions such as `time`, `lat`, and `lon`.

```{r load-data}
data_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dblaskey/ML_Course_Code/main/Data/sst.nc"
file_path <- "sst.nc"

if (!file.exists(file_path)) {
  download.file(data_url, destfile = file_path, mode = "wb")
}

sst_rast <- rast(file_path)
sst_rast
```

The SST variable is stored as a multilayer raster. Each layer represents one time step.

```{r inspect-raster}
nlyr(sst_rast)
ext(sst_rast)
res(sst_rast)
time(sst_rast)
```

# 3. Convert Gridded Data to a Machine-Learning Table

Most `tidymodels` workflows expect a table where each row is one observation. Here, one row will represent one grid cell at one time. The target is `sst`. The predictors will be simple features based on location, season, and time.

```{r raster-to-table}
# Convert raster layers to a wide table with x/y columns and one column per time step.
sst_wide <- as.data.frame(sst_rast, xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(lon = x, lat = y)

# Use raster time metadata when available.
sst_dates <- time(sst_rast)

# Pivot from wide raster format to long machine-learning format.
df <- sst_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(lon, lat),
    names_to = "layer",
    values_to = "sst"
  ) %>%
  drop_na(sst) %>%
  mutate(
    layer_index = as.integer(factor(layer, levels = names(sst_rast))),
    time = sst_dates[layer_index],
    year = lubridate::year(time),
    month = lubridate::month(time),
    time_index = (year - min(year, na.rm = TRUE)) * 12 + (month - 1),
    month_sin = sin(2 * pi * month / 12),
    month_cos = cos(2 * pi * month / 12),
    lon_sin = sin(2 * pi * lon / 360),
    lon_cos = cos(2 * pi * lon / 360)
  )

dim(df)
head(df)
```

## TODO: Historical Monthly SST Feature

Create a historical average SST feature for each location and month. Be careful not to use future data when creating this column.

The idea is:

1. Group by location and month.
2. Sort by time.
3. Compute the cumulative mean from previous observations only.
4. Use `lag()` so the current observation is not used to predict itself.

```{r historical-monthly-feature}
# TODO: Create Month_Average_sst without using future data.
# Hint: use lag(cummean(sst)).

# Example scaffold:
df <- df %>%
   group_by(lat, lon, month) %>%
   mutate(Month_Average_sst = dplyr::lag(cummean(sst))) %>%
   ungroup()

df <- df %>%
  drop_na(Month_Average_sst)

```

# 4. Define the Prediction Problem

We will predict SST from simple location and time features. This is not meant to be the best possible ocean forecasting model. The goal is to study how evaluation changes when data are spatially and temporally correlated.

```{r prediction-problem}
feature_cols <- c(
  "lat",
  "lon_sin",
  "lon_cos",
  "month_sin",
  "month_cos",
  "time_index",
  "Month_Average_sst"
)

target_col <- "sst"

# If Month_Average_sst does not exist yet, stop with a helpful reminder.
stopifnot("Month_Average_sst" %in% names(df))

model_data <- df %>%
  select(all_of(c(target_col, feature_cols, "year", "lat", "lon", "time"))) %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number())

head(model_data)
```

# 5. Create a Reusable Model Workflow

We will use a tree-based regression model. Tree-based models can capture nonlinear patterns such as warmer temperatures near the equator and seasonal variation.

In `tidymodels`, we define:

- a **recipe** for preprocessing,
- a **model specification**, and
- a **workflow** that combines them.

```{r workflow}
sst_recipe <- recipe(sst ~ lat + lon_sin + lon_cos + month_sin + month_cos + time_index + Month_Average_sst,
                     data = model_data) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors())

rf_spec <- rand_forest(
  trees = 300,
  min_n = 5,
  mtry = 4
) %>%
  set_mode("regression") %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity")

sst_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(sst_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_spec)

sst_workflow
```

```{r helper-functions}
summarize_resamples <- function(resample_results, label) {
  collect_metrics(resample_results) %>%
    select(.metric, mean, std_err) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = .metric,
      values_from = c(mean, std_err)
    ) %>%
    transmute(
      Evaluation = label,
      `Mean RMSE` = mean_rmse,
      `SE RMSE` = std_err_rmse,
      `Mean MAE` = mean_mae,
      `Mean R2` = mean_rsq
    )
}

regression_metrics <- metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq)
```

# 6. Naive Evaluation: Random k-Fold Cross-Validation

Random k-fold cross-validation mixes observations from different locations and times into each fold. This is common in introductory machine learning, but it is often too optimistic for spatial-temporal data because very similar observations may appear in both training and test folds.


```{r random-cv}
random_cv <- vfold_cv(model_data, v = 5)

random_results <- fit_resamples(
  sst_workflow,
  resamples = random_cv,
  metrics = regression_metrics,
  control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)
)

collect_metrics(random_results)
```

```{r random-summary}
random_summary <- summarize_resamples(random_results, "Random k-fold CV")
random_summary
```

# 7. Temporal Block Cross-Validation

Now we will hold out entire years. This asks a different question:

> Can the model generalize to years it has not seen during training?

This is a better approximation of forecasting or prediction into future time periods than random cross-validation.

```{r temporal-block-cv}
# TODO: Complete temporal block cross-validation.

# Step 1: create grouped folds by year.
temporal_cv <- group_vfold_cv(model_data,  group = year, v=5) # replace NULL with group_vfold_cv(...)

# Step 2: run blocked cross-validation.
temporal_results <-  fit_resamples(
  sst_workflow,
  resamples = temporal_cv,
  metrics = regression_metrics,
  control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)
) # replace NULL with fit_resamples(...)

# Step 3: display the results.
temporal_results
```

# 8. Spatial Block Cross-Validation

Now we will hold out entire regions. This asks:

> Can the model generalize to locations it has not seen during training?

Spatial blocking is useful when your real prediction task involves mapping unsampled locations or transferring a model to a new region.

## TODO: Variogram of Residuals

Use cross-validated residuals from the random CV model to estimate the spatial scale of residual autocorrelation. This avoids using purely in-sample residuals, which can understate model error.

**Hint:** Look back at the earlier spatial regression activity. One reasonable approach is:

1. Fit the workflow once to the full modeling table.
2. Predict SST for the same rows.
3. Convert to overall average observed and modeled sst for each location.
4. Compute residuals.
5. Convert into an `sf`/`sp` object.
6. Use `gstat::variogram()`.

```{r residual-variogram, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# TODO: Create a variogram of model residuals to estimate spatial autocorrelation distance. 

random_predictions <- collect_predictions(random_results)

residual_data <- random_predictions %>%
  mutate(residual = sst - .pred) %>%
  left_join(
    model_data %>%
      mutate(.row = row_number()) %>%
      select(.row, lat, lon, time),
    by = ".row"
  )

residual_one_time <- residual_data %>%
  filter(time == min(time)) %>%
  sample_n(size = min(3000, n()))

residual_sf <- st_as_sf(
  residual_one_time,
  coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  crs = 4326
) %>%
  st_transform(3857)

residual_sp <- as(residual_sf, "Spatial")

residual_variogram <- variogram(residual ~ 1, data = residual_sp)

plot(residual_variogram, main = "Variogram of cross-validated residuals")
```

## Create Spatial Blocks

Once you have estimated the extent of spatial autocorrelation, use that information to set the block size.

```{r create-spatial-blocks}
# TODO: choose block sizes based on your variogram or exploratory reasoning.
lat_block_size <- 5 # replace NULL with a numeric block size, such as 5
lon_block_size <- 5 # replace NULL with a numeric block size, such as 5

model_data <- model_data %>%
  mutate(
    lat_block = floor((lat + 90) / lat_block_size),
    lon_block = floor(lon / lon_block_size),
    spatial_block = paste(lat_block, lon_block, sep = "_")
  )

cat("Number of spatial blocks:", n_distinct(model_data$spatial_block), "\n")

model_data %>%
  select(lat, lon, lat_block, lon_block, spatial_block) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  head()
```

# 9. Spatial-Temporal Holdout

Spatial blocking asks whether the model can generalize to new places. Temporal blocking asks whether the model can generalize to new years. A spatial-temporal holdout combines both ideas.

Here we create a stricter test: the test data must come from held-out spatial blocks **and** held-out years. The training data exclude those spatial blocks and those years.

```{r strict-spatiotemporal-function}
make_strict_spatiotemporal_splits <- function(data, spatial_col = "spatial_block", time_col = "year", v = 5) {
  spatial_blocks <- sort(unique(data[[spatial_col]]))
  time_blocks <- sort(unique(data[[time_col]]))

  spatial_fold_ids <- sample(rep(seq_len(v), length.out = length(spatial_blocks)))
  time_fold_ids <- sample(rep(seq_len(v), length.out = length(time_blocks)))

  spatial_lookup <- tibble(
    spatial_block_value = spatial_blocks,
    spatial_fold = spatial_fold_ids
  )

  time_lookup <- tibble(
    time_block_value = time_blocks,
    time_fold = time_fold_ids
  )

  split_list <- vector("list", v)

  for (fold_id in seq_len(v)) {
    heldout_spatial <- spatial_lookup %>%
      filter(spatial_fold == fold_id) %>%
      pull(spatial_block_value)

    heldout_time <- time_lookup %>%
      filter(time_fold == fold_id) %>%
      pull(time_block_value)

    assessment_idx <- which(data[[spatial_col]] %in% heldout_spatial & data[[time_col]] %in% heldout_time)
    analysis_idx <- which(!(data[[spatial_col]] %in% heldout_spatial) & !(data[[time_col]] %in% heldout_time))

    split_list[[fold_id]] <- make_splits(
      list(analysis = analysis_idx, assessment = assessment_idx),
      data = data
    )
  }

  manual_rset(
    splits = split_list,
    ids = paste0("Fold", seq_len(v))
  )
}
```

```{r strict-spatiotemporal-cv}
strict_st_cv <- make_strict_spatiotemporal_splits(
  model_data,
  spatial_col = "spatial_block",
  time_col = "year",
  v = 5
)

strict_st_results <- fit_resamples(
  sst_workflow,
  resamples = strict_st_cv,
  metrics = regression_metrics,
  control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)
)

collect_metrics(strict_st_results)
```

```{r strict-spatiotemporal-summary}
strict_st_summary <- summarize_resamples(strict_st_results, "Spatial-temporal block CV")
strict_st_summary
```

## Discussion: Spatial-Temporal Holdout

The spatial-temporal holdout is the hardest evaluation in this homework because the model is asked to predict observations from a region and years that were excluded from training.

If this error is much larger than the random CV error, that is not a failure of the model. It is evidence that the original random CV estimate was answering an easier question.
